themes.theme: Cross-government communities, networks and central support
themes.definition: Standing groups and networks that connect people working on AI across departments, and central bodies offering support to them.

UK136 asks procurement teams to establish networks within the organisation and across the civil service, align with teams leading on AI initiatives and use procurement strategically through collaboration and shared knowledge. UK082 proposes that DSIT, as 'the digital centre of government', support public sector partners where needed, without saying what form the support takes. Participation is always voluntary, and the passages do not name who organises the main groups or what they produce.

themes.theme: Recording and passing on lessons, and reuse
themes.definition: Practices for capturing what was learned from AI projects and pilots, and for making work reusable across teams and organisations.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK099 encourages teams to record and publish lessons learned (per the note, on managing privacy risks and on public attitudes) in internal knowledge bases, and AI_Insights asks developers to allow time to document and share learnings and to schedule knowledge-sharing sessions and expert surgeries to avoid duplicated effort. UK071 says departments can tailor its testing framework and contribute their learning back into a shared understanding of how to evaluate AI responsibly, without naming the receiving mechanism. UK266 says mechanisms 'are needed' so that insights from pilots are disseminated and used to improve future pilots, without saying who provides them, and UK010 (Ofgem) suggests forums and communities of practice for sharing lessons. UK136 asks for open, reusable work, and UK082 recommends mandating interoperable infrastructure, reusable modular code and open-sourcing. Apart from UK082's proposed mandate, sharing is encouraged rather than required, and no passage asks that the results of testing or evaluating a particular tool be shared; UK071's learning about how to evaluate is the closest.

themes.theme: Engaging and informing the public, civil society, affected groups and other stakeholders
themes.definition: Requirements to consult, involve or communicate with people outside the project team, from staff and end users to civil society, equality groups and those most likely to be affected.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 is the strongest: when defining and deploying AI, 'you must understand people’s needs and priorities by conducting user research and engaging with the public as appropriate', including (per the note) civil society groups, under-represented individuals and those most likely to experience harm; it also asks for an engagement plan at the start, an AI communication strategy, governance that works with civil society organisations, and seeking and documenting the views of people whose personal data is processed. UK216 (EHRC) asks public bodies to talk to staff, service users, equality groups and community groups, to involve equality groups before and after implementation, and to gather evidence from organisations that have used similar products. UK268 lists early and ongoing stakeholder engagement through workshops, citizen assemblies or public consultations, joint development of project objectives with the project owner and stakeholders, and clear communication of the system's purpose to end users, IT staff and management. UK099 asks teams to involve diverse stakeholders, including those most affected, in design and testing and to ask people what transparency they would find meaningful; UK010 (Ofgem) asks that governance arrangements be communicated to those affected and that excluded consumers be reached by other means. Engagement is framed as an input to design and assessment; no passage says how what is heard must change the tool, and only UK174's 'must' rises above recommendation.

themes.theme: Feedback loops from users, operators and stakeholders
themes.definition: Channels through which the people who use, operate or are affected by a tool can report problems with it or shape it on a continuing basis.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK099 recommends a feedback loop in which users and operators identify issues and send them back to the development team, and, where appropriate, engaging civil society organisations on how to design feedback and redress mechanisms. UK099 also recommends feedback mechanisms such as surveys and advisory boards so stakeholders can continuously shape project outcomes. UK071 lists collecting feedback from users, operators and impacted stakeholders as a core practice of continuous monitoring; the coder note records interface flags such as 'this output seems wrong' or 'Did this help?', with flagged cases reviewed in retrospectives or sprint planning. This is the main route in the cell by which an error in an individual output might reach a human, but it depends on a user noticing and reporting it [inference].

themes.theme: Links between evaluators, testers and the teams that build, run and govern the tool
themes.definition: Arrangements that connect those evaluating or testing an AI tool with its developers, the designers of the intervention, end users, evaluation specialists and the people who decide on its use.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK133, on evaluating the impact of AI interventions, asks evaluators to work closely with the team developing the AI tool, the team designing the intervention and end users when building the Theory of Change, to work with stakeholders to find existing data for a baseline, to identify possible differential impacts on groups using input from designers and evidence from assurance exercises, to align evaluation phases with design and deployment, and to consult departmental evaluation experts. For generative AI it says this 'could' involve working with the development team to sample the outputs the tool generates over the course of the intervention. UK071, a testing framework, says the bias and fairness module's results 'should be reviewed by both technical teams and policy/legal teams', and that the testing team's recommendation will feed governance decision-making in the next phase, as advice rather than authority. These are the most direct passages in the cell on checking outputs, but they say who should work with whom, not what outputs are compared against or what level is acceptable.

themes.theme: Coordination among regulators and with central government

It describes a DSIT central function whose roles include supporting coherence across regulators, promoting information sharing and reviewing gaps in regulatory powers and remits, with a planned third phase of collaborative work on joint tools; parts of this were planned rather than in effect. themes.theme: Building the AI assurance ecosystem: standards, accreditation and convening
themes.definition: Efforts to connect standards bodies, accreditation and professional bodies, regulators, policy teams and industry around AI assurance as a market and a profession.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK207 commits the Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation (CDEI) to support the AI Standards Hub being set up by the DCMS Digital Standards team and the Office for AI, to convene an AI assurance accreditation forum of professional and accreditation bodies, to run events building a cross-stakeholder strategy 'and corresponding accountabilities', to advise regulators and policy teams, and to work in partnership with policy teams, regulators, industry and professional bodies. It also commits CDEI to embed assurance thinking in partnership projects with defence-focused organisations, police forces and local authorities, the one passage here directly about public bodies, with form and outputs not stated, and says 'a coordinated effort is required' among ecosystem actors. UK206 states that it is UK government policy that third-party conformity assessment services be obtained from organisations accredited by UKAS, and suggests that private sector organisations, particularly SMEs, engage with standards bodies such as BSI. These passages build the supply side of assurance; public bodies appear mainly as partners, not as buyers of assurance for their own tools [inference].

not_themed.reason: Off-topic: an email address for feedback on the Ofgem guidance document itself, not a mechanism connecting actors around an AI tool (the coder note says as much).

Off-topic: about restructuring how NAO publications are published so that other people's AI tools can read them, not about governing an AI tool used in the public sector (flagged as an edge case in the coder note).

absences: Every starting code for Coordination has passages, but unevenly (themes across all three parts). Shared templates appear only as the ATRS template; no passage provides a shared template for supplier information (such as a model card), for test plans or for incident reports. Registers are the public ATRS repository and internal inventories; there is no register of incidents, errors or test results, and no passage links internal inventories to the ATRS repository. Referrals between bodies are thin: the only binding one is restated statute (prior consultation of the ICO), and most 'referrals' are to teams inside the same organisation. Cross-government groups are named, but their organiser, rules (beyond the GOV.UK email limit for the AI security group) and outputs are not. A reader would also expect, and the passages do not provide: a route for reporting errors or failures in AI outputs across government (the one mandatory reporting chain, in UK190, covers misuse and security incidents inside one department); any duty on a supplier to notify the buyer when a model or its version changes (the closest are UK190's duty to inform DWP when AI is incorporated into services and the ATRS model-version field); any mechanism for sharing the results of testing or evaluating a specific tool between bodies; any stated purpose or follow-up for the public contact points; and, apart from UK190's disciplinary consequence for failing to report security incidents and the ICO consultation that must precede processing, any stated consequence if a coordination requirement is not met.
cross_cutting: The supply chain dominates this cell: roughly a third or more of the passages concern how a public body buys AI and what it extracts from or imposes on suppliers, through procurement rules, contract terms, information requests, data-sharing terms and the supplier fields of the ATRS record. The other large clusters are consultation of in-house specialists, engagement with the public and stakeholders, and the ATRS hub-and-spoke link between public bodies and the central ATRS team, which, with UK190's chain of reporting duties inside DWP, is the most fully specified mechanism. Binding force is low: most passages use 'should', 'consider' or 'encouraged' in non-statutory guidance, 'must' appears in UK174 and UK099 guidance without stated enforcement, in UK190 as departmental policy, and in restated statute (procurement law, international data transfers, prior consultation of the ICO), and consequences are almost never stated. The holder is overwhelmingly the deploying body or project team addressed as 'you'; suppliers appear as counterparties whose duties depend on what the buyer writes into the contract (UK190 is the exception), and central bodies (the ATRS team in DSIT, a DSIT central function for regulators, CDEI, the NAO) act as hubs whose powers over others are mostly not stated. On checking AI outputs, coordination passages say who should talk to whom much more often than what is checked: the substantive measures are the questions put to suppliers before purchase (accuracy, hallucination rates, differential performance across groups, performance on the buyer's local data), UK071's requirement that bias test results be reviewed by technical and policy/legal teams before a governance decision, UK133's suggestion to sample generative AI outputs with the development team, and AI_Insights' tiered bias alerts with escalation to decision-makers. No passage sets a threshold, and none addresses consistency or repeatability of outputs, prompts or configuration, or confidence scores; model version appears only as an ATRS record field. The route by which an individual wrong output reaches a human is user and operator feedback (UK099, UK071) or a public contact address whose purpose is not stated.
